extracted.intended_audience: educated general readers and travelers interested in social, political, and industrial commentary
extracted.subtask_short: travelogue observations on education and Paris
extracted.subtask_description: A mid-19th-century travelogue/report combining first-person travel narrative (London–Paris), observations of the Great Exhibition/Crystal Palace, and normative commentary on popular education, religion, commerce, and French politics and society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exhibition as contributor to Industrial and Practical Education
rubrics_metrics.description: The Exhibition is destined to contribute immensely to the Industrial and Practical Education of the British People.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A large proportion of mechanics, artisans and apprentices will visit and compare their trade's products with those of other nations; even if only a minority profit intellectually, fifty thousand skilled artisans or apprentices returning home informed can work great triumphs. The text emphasizes that comparison stimulates discernment of where one's work has 'comparatively failed.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Adoption and adaptation of labor-saving machinery
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple adaptation of the forces now attained, the principles established, the machines already invented, to beneficent uses would speedily transform the industrial and social condition of mankind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific expectation that machinery could greatly reduce labor (example: 'Boots and Shoes may be cut out and made up by machinery with less than one-fourth the labor now required'); sewing plain seams on thick cloth should be mechanized; the Exhibition should be followed by immense advances in labor-saving machinery, especially in Britain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common schools funded by property taxation as a public good
rubrics_metrics.description: A well managed system of Common Schools, supported by taxation on Property, would save more in diminishing the burden of Pauperism than it would cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The nation is wealthy and public-spirited and many influential classes realize this, yet political forces (e.g., votes in the House of Commons) block implementation. The practical criterion is fiscal: the cost is justified by social savings and reduced pauperism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clerical responsibility and non-obstruction of secular education (Episcopal critique)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Episcopal priesthood (and similar established clergy) is chiefly responsible for obstructing a system of Common Schools by insisting on recognition of their creeds in a national system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative demand that clergy 'Teach the children as much Religion as you can; very few of you ever lack pupils when you give your hearts to the work' and if they truly wanted religious instruction they should not block secular instruction. The guidance asserts that state-paid clergy should perform their religious duties rather than prevent secular schooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catholic clergy: teach dogma out of school-hours and accept secular schools
rubrics_metrics.description: Catholic clergy should require that dogmas be taught out of school-hours and be content that no antagonist dogmas are taught in secular schools.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acknowledges Catholics receive no state support and therefore may distrust the state; still, the recommended practice to enable a national common-school system is to confine sectarian instruction to non-school hours. Example reasoning: if Catholic clergy established good common schools in countries where they are dominant, their opposition in Britain would be more excusable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards for preparing dried fruits for export
rubrics_metrics.description: To succeed exporting dried fruits (apples, peaches) to England, products must be dried perfectly, prepared with scrupulous neatness, and packed in clean wooden boxes of standard sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advice that time and expenditure are required to make these products known to British consumers and to assure them of cleanliness; casual or miscellaneous exportation risks loss. Suggested box sizes: twenty-five, fifty and one hundred pounds. Also notes use of cheap land and labor (aged persons and children) for production, with potential to draw on other regions in bountiful years.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate conveyance standards for cross-Channel passenger service
rubrics_metrics.description: Passenger boats on the Dover–Calais route should be decent and seaworthy; the current long, black, narrow scow-like steamboats are unfit for such important service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism that existing boats cause widespread sea-sickness and discomfort (three fourths of passengers sick on the author's crossing); a good boat could make the passage comfortable even in a smart breeze and 'cannot reputably be withheld.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in national commerce and avoiding mortgaging essentials for luxuries
rubrics_metrics.description: A nation should not buy more wares and fabrics than its exports will pay for, nor trade away essential and imperishable assets for factitious and transitory goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: the farmer who 'drinks up his farm' despite apparently getting more for his exports has done a pernicious, losing business. The savage tribe exchanging hunting grounds for liquor is another example. The thrifty household is held as the true model of the nation. The text argues that persistent trade deficits that consume specie or mortgage land are harmful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism toward manufactured petitions and requirement of universal suffrage to gauge public will
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitions for constitutional revision gathered by local officials, employers, and government employees do not reliably reflect the people's true wishes; to know the people's desire, the restrictive May 31st law disfranchising three million electors must be repealed (restore universal suffrage).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains mechanisms of how signatures are procured (prefects, mayors, employers) and why such petitions are unrepresentative; the recommended standard for legitimacy is enfranchisement of the whole people so their genuine preferences can be measured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political durability criterion for the French Republic
rubrics_metrics.description: The Republic cannot be legally subverted by the reactionary minority because they lack the necessary representative majority; time and endurance strengthen the Republican cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: while reactionary groups (Bourbonists, Orleanists, Bonapartists) may combine to a few million, they are far fewer than the thirty million in the nation; prolonged nominal republicanism makes return to monarchy more difficult. Also, attempts to change constitution without restoring suffrage lack legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of Parisian social character (amusement-centered life)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parisian social life is intensely sociable and centered on amusement; while people are intelligent, vivacious and generous, they are also impulsive, fickle, sensual and irreverent — 'Paris is the Paradise of the Senses; a focus of Enjoyment, not of Happiness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observations: eating/drinking alone is rare, theaters and concerts are nightly necessities, public amusements are abundant and socially central; consequences include high proportions of unmarried, decaying families, and many births out of wedlock. Philanthropic and educational civic activity is less frequent than in London.
